explanations: luna: The source's camels come to a water stop; here each of the twelve groups is given a known drinking place (مَشْرَبَهُمْ), making a settled, allotted water station part of a people's journey. | terra: Twelve springs emerge and every people knows its drinking-place; the allocated water-stop parallels the she-camel's known turn without itself mentioning mounts.
terra: The required cow is explicitly untrained for plowing or watering fields; this gives a Qur'anic animal counterpart to the source-section's hard mount that has not yet been trained for work.

luna: The source develops ر غ ب as a wide-striding horse and as desire directed to the Lord; this ayah uses the root for turning away from Abraham's way, a specific reversal of the source's directed desire, though the sense is distinct. | terra: مَن يَرْغَبُ عَن مِّلَّةِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ uses رغبة with “away from”; it clarifies by reversal the directional force of desiring toward the Lord.
terra: Ships run through the sea carrying what benefits people; burden-bearing transport is placed among the signs of providentially ordered creation.

luna: The source uses عُسْر and يُسْر for a hard versus yielding mount; this ayah pairs the same roots in fasting and says God intends ease, not hardship, giving the image a concrete case of religious ease. | terra: God wills اليُسْر and does not will العُسْر; the legal context states as divine intention the opposition that the section embodies as two kinds of mount.

luna: The source's caravan bears loads for its journey; this pilgrimage ayah tells travelers to take provisions and calls God-consciousness the best provision, applying the load image to the Hajj road.

luna: The source says that after one task is finished, effort and desire turn toward God; this Hajj ayah describes departing Arafat, seeking bounty from the Lord, and remembering Him at the sacred landmark.
terra: The prayer asks the Lord not to place a crushing obligation upon the speakers or load them beyond capacity; it voices the human side of the burden the section says was removed.

terra: Fine horses and livestock are objects of worldly desire, while the verse ends by locating the good return with God; attachment to the mount is set against desire directed toward the final destination.

luna: The source's effort is a journey toward God; this ayah groups migration, expulsion, harm suffered in God's cause, and a promised Garden, placing travel and hardship within a path of divine reward.
terra: God wishes to lighten the human burden because humanity was created weak; it states the mercy that the section renders as weight removed from a strained back.

luna: The source's road ends in turning toward the Lord; this ayah promises a wide route and refuge in the earth to one who migrates toward God and His Messenger. | terra: The emigrant finds wide places and abundance in the earth, and one who leaves home toward God and His Messenger has an assured reward even if death overtakes him; the road is broad and its direction divine.

luna: The source's animal journey arrives at a sacred destination; this ayah protects sacrificial offerings and garlanded animals while people travel toward the Sacred House seeking God's bounty and approval.

luna: The source's ن ص ب branch describes effort and an upright stance; this ayah's النُّصُب names erected altars where animals are sacrificed, a distinct lexical sense that marks the boundary between a working mount and an animal at a ritual station.
terra: God does not intend to place constriction upon believers; this gives the hard/easy mount image a legal and purifying counterpart.

luna: The source reads the surah's back as a camel carrying another's load; this ayah depicts deniers carrying their own burdens on their backs at the Hour (يَحْمِلُونَ أَوْزَارَهُمْ عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِمْ), reversing useful cargo into the consequence of one's deeds. | terra: The lost carry their أَوْزَارَهُمْ عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِمْ; the same burden-and-back configuration turns people into the load-bearing animals of their own wrongdoing.

luna: The source's pack camel bears a load; this ayah divides livestock into “carriers” (حَمُولَةً) and low-to-ground animals, directly naming the load-bearing class. | terra: God creates from livestock حَمُولَةً, animals of burden; this is the Qur'anic category to which the section's load-bearing caravan beast belongs.

luna: The source's pack camel can bear someone else's physical load; this ayah draws the boundary that no soul bears another's moral burden, then says return is to the Lord, distinguishing carried cargo from personal accountability. | terra: No bearer carries another's burden, and the verse ends with return to “your Lord”; distribution of loads and the journey's divine endpoint appear together.

luna: The source's camel is a workable mount even when difficult to train; this ayah uses a camel entering a needle's eye (الْجَمَلُ فِي سَمِّ الْخِيَاطِ) as an impossible threshold, reversing the animal's role as a means of passage. | terra: The camel cannot pass through a needle's eye; the broad load-bearing traveler meets an aperture that no gait or tractability can overcome.

luna: The source gives a camel its place in a journey; Salih's people are shown God's she-camel as a sign, opening another Quranic camel scene. | terra: Allah's she-camel is left to graze on God's earth; it directly supplies the section's camel remaining in pasture and frames that access as a sign.

luna: The source's camel bears people through the road; this continuation says the Thamud hamstrung the she-camel, making destruction of the animal a reversal of the source's useful mount. | terra: The people hamstring the she-camel after her protected pasture is announced; they destroy the very animal entrusted to them as a sign and provision.

luna: The source uses وَضَعَ for lowering a camel's neck and setting a load down; this ayah says the Messenger removes burdens and shackles (وَيَضَعُ عَنْهُمْ إِصْرَهُمْ وَالْأَغْلَالَ), turning the load image toward relief. | terra: The Messenger يَضَعُ عَنْهُمْ إِصْرَهُمْ, removing people's burden from them; its syntax and relief closely match the section's load being put down from the addressed traveler.

luna: This repeated account again gives each group its own drinking place (مَشْرَبَهُمْ); it confirms the water-stop scene of 2:60 and adds the setting of Israel's wilderness provision. | terra: Each of the twelve tribes knows its drinking-place and receives shade and food; ordered access to water is embedded in a fuller scene of travel provision.
terra: At Badr the believers occupy one side of the valley, the enemy the other, and the caravan is lower down; a moving caravan is located precisely within the road-landscape.
terra: God now lightens the believers' demand after acknowledging weakness among them; capacity determines how much weight is laid upon the traveler.

luna: The source sends the traveler onto a demanding road toward God; this ayah rebukes those who “cling heavily to the earth” (ٱثَّاقَلْتُمْ إِلَى ٱلْأَرْضِ) when told to march, explicitly contrasting departure with attachment to the nearer life.

luna: The source camel carries concrete loads on the road; this command to go forth “light or heavy” (خِفَافًا وَثِقَالًا) addresses expeditionaries' conditions, so the load echo is specific but not certainly literal cargo.

luna: The source contrasts the difficult, untrained mount with the easy one; this ayah contrasts an easy gain and short journey with the believers' long, hard expedition, giving the same easy/difficult polarity a travel context. | terra: A near gain and moderate journey would have drawn the hypocrites, but the distance seemed hard; willingness is exposed by how demanding the road appears.
luna: The source's rider says his mount is prepared for riding; this ayah says the hypocrites would have prepared supplies if they truly intended to set out, reversing readiness for travel.

luna: The source dictionary branch B003 of و ض ع describes an easy pace and its contrast with faster movement; the verse's لَأَوْضَعُوا۟ uses that root for the hypocrites' rapid riding through the ranks, giving the pace word a disruptive social setting. | terra: وَلَأَوْضَعُوا خِلَالَكُمْ uses the section's gait-root for harmful rushing among the believers; the easy-paced dictionary branch is sharply redirected into disruptive speed.

luna: The source dictionary says “my mount is ready to ride”; this ayah describes people asking the Prophet for mounts, then leaving in tears when none can be found, showing travel depends on provision. | terra: Those who ask the Prophet for mounts weep when none can be found to carry them; the absent ride reveals how decisive the section's load-bearing gift is for a journey.

luna: The source's B004 branch of ن ص ب is travel-weariness; this ayah names thirst, fatigue (نَصَب), and hunger endured on God's path as good deeds, giving the loaded road spiritual value. | terra: Road thirst and نَصَب are credited as righteous work, while وَلَا يَرْغَبُوا links that fatigue to directed preference; both of the section's final roots operate in one journey.

luna: The source's day-long caravan walk is measured effort; this continuation records every expense and valley crossed by the believers, completing 9:120's account of rewarded travel hardship. | terra: Every valley the travelers cross is credited to them as a righteous deed; it continues 9:120 by making the actual ground covered part of the rewarded fatigue.
terra: God carries people over land and sea, but favorable travel turns into a storm in which they call on Him sincerely; the journey-prayer arises under threat rather than after calmly mounting.
terra: The ark's course and anchorage are both in God's name; an alternate vehicle has its movement and settled endpoint held by Rabb, like the section's caravan.
terra: The flood subsides and the ark settles on Judi; this supplies the actual resting-place toward which the course and anchorage of 11:41 were directed.

luna: The source's camel reaches a place to drink; Salih points to God's she-camel and says she has her turn at the water, another explicit water-sharing scene. | terra: The same she-camel is to feed freely in God's earth and remain unharmed; the pasture is a protected provision rather than mere scenery.

luna: The source's camel is a useful mount and carrier; the next ayah reports that Salih's people hamstrung the water-sharing camel, the opposite fate for a working animal. | terra: After the command to let the she-camel graze, they hamstring her and receive a final three-day respite; settled pasture turns into irreversible departure.
terra: Pharaoh leads his people into the Fire and it is called an evil watering-place; a leader's herd-like arrival at water becomes the opposite of safe guidance and refreshment.

luna: The source builds a caravan and a water stop; this ayah has a caravan arrive and send its water-drawer to lower a bucket, joining travel, water, and the discovery of a carried human being. | terra: A caravan halts and sends its water-drawer, who lowers his bucket; it joins caravan movement to the water-stop developed in the section.
terra: Joseph fully provisions the travelers and then conditions their next return; caravan equipment and the future road are planned together.
terra: The travelers' merchandise is put into their رِحَال, the very saddle-baggage named in the source section's creaking-load definition.
terra: The brothers ask for an added كَيْلَ بَعِيرٍ and call it كَيْلٌ يَسِيرٌ; a camel-load and ease meet explicitly inside a provisioned caravan.
terra: Joseph places the drinking cup in his brother's رَحْل after loading the travelers; saddle-baggage and water equipment meet in one caravan act.
terra: The reward is حِمْلُ بَعِيرٍ, a camel-load of grain; the mount's carrying capacity becomes the unit of promised provision.
terra: The brothers appeal to the caravan in which they returned as a witness; the عِير is a travelling community, not only a set of animals.
terra: When the caravan departs, Jacob senses Joseph's scent; the moment of setting out makes the caravan carry news before its riders arrive.
terra: God subjects ships to run by His command and subjects the rivers; the journey's vehicle and waterway are both made tractable.
terra: Paradise contains no نَصَب and its people are never expelled; it precisely combines release from journey-weariness with the section's final place that is never left.
luna: The source treats the loaded camel as a mercy of animal travel; this ayah names livestock's warmth, other benefits, and food, filling out the material provision behind that journey.

luna: The source's camels move between pasture and watering/resting places; this ayah describes livestock returning home in the evening and being driven out to pasture in the morning, giving the route a daily rhythm. | terra: Livestock have beauty when brought home and when sent out to pasture; the two daily movements supply the section's stopping and grazing life around the road.

luna: The source's dictionary branch for ظ ه ر makes the back a riding beast carrying loads; this ayah explicitly has animals bear heavy loads to a distant town that people could reach only with hardship, joining the caravan's burden and difficult road to a divine mercy. | terra: The livestock carry human loads to a land reachable only with severe strain; this is the section's laden journey-animal, while the closing mercy identifies the mount itself as divine relief.

luna: The source's mount is a prepared animal for riding; this ayah names horses, mules, and donkeys made for riding and adornment, extending the caravan's set of mounts. | terra: Horses, mules, and donkeys are created لِتَرْكَبُوهَا; it extends the load-bearing mercy of 16:7 into the explicit act of riding.

luna: The source's camels stop for water and pasture; this ayah pairs drinkable rainwater with plants in which livestock graze (فِيهِ تُسِيمُونَ), directly supplying both parts of that stop. | terra: God sends water from which people drink and vegetation in which they pasture animals; watering and grazing are joined as road-side provision.

luna: The source's caravan needs a route and stopping landscape; this ayah places firm mountains, rivers, and paths in the earth so people can be guided through it. | terra: God places landmarks and roads so people may be guided; these are the divinely fitted ways on which the section's caravan can travel.
luna: This continuation adds landmarks and stars as guides, completing the route-finding scene of 16:15 and giving the source's road a way to be followed.
terra: Misleaders carry their own burdens and some burdens of those they misled; moral influence becomes an added load rather than the removed burden of the section.

luna: The source dictionary's root ن ق ض pictures journeys as if they dismantled the camel; this ayah warns against a woman who unravels her firmly spun yarn, a direct reversal of held-together work into undoing. | terra: The woman who unravels her yarn after it was strong gives نَقْض its physical dismantling force; it clarifies the source-section claim that long journeys seem to unravel the camel.
terra: The rule that no burdened soul bears another's burden repeats the moral limit implicit in the section's individualized load.
terra: The arrogant walker can neither split the earth nor reach the mountains in height; human pretension cannot turn an elevated gait into true elevation.
terra: Satan is told to incite with his voice and rally his cavalry and infantry; voice and mounted force form a dark reversal of the rider's guiding sound and Godward travel.
terra: The Lord drives ships through the sea so travelers can seek His bounty, and the verse names His mercy toward them; conveyance, provision, and Rabb's care coincide.

luna: The source's caravan carries people along a road; this ayah says humanity is carried on land and sea and provided good things, widening the transport image beyond camels. | terra: Human beings are carried on land and sea and supplied with good things; carriage and road provision are presented together as honor.

luna: The source's caravan has a destination that gives its long walk direction; Moses says he will not stop until reaching the meeting of the two seas, the goal later followed by the travel-fatigue of 18:62. | terra: Moses refuses to cease travelling until he reaches the meeting of the seas; sustained road effort is ordered by a fixed destination.
terra: At the confluence the travelers forget the fish and it takes its path into the sea; this is the missed arrival whose consequences produce the fatigue named in 18:62.

luna: The source dictionary branch B004 for ن ص ب describes exhaustion from remaining upright; Moses' companion calls their journey's fatigue نَصَبًا, while 18:60 supplies the long journey's goal. | terra: After passing the meeting place, Moses names what the section stages: لَقِينَا مِن سَفَرِنَا هَٰذَا نَصَبًا, fatigue encountered through travel.
terra: The servant recalls their rest at the rock and the fish's extraordinary path; a stopping-place, forgotten provision, and route-recognition meet here.
terra: Moses identifies the sought place and the pair retrace their footprints; reaching the true destination requires turning back along the road already travelled.
terra: The wall يُرِيدُ أَن يَنقَضَّ, is about to collapse; this physical giving-way is the closest Qur'anic parallel to the worn mount seemingly broken apart by travel.
terra: Abraham's father asks whether he is turning away, أَرَاغِبٌ أَنتَ عَنْ آلِهَتِي; this false-godward threat sharpens the section's opposite orientation toward Rabb.
terra: Moses asks his Lord to make his task easy; prophetic work is imagined as something whose difficulty can be rendered tractable.

luna: The source's broad road is a physical route across the earth; this ayah says God made paths there for people to travel, adding a landscape to the caravan image. | terra: God spreads the earth and threads it with roads before bringing out pasture; route and grazing-ground form the terrain completed in 20:54.

luna: The source names pasture as where camels remain; this ayah commands people to eat and pasture their livestock (وَارْعَوْا أَنْعَامَكُمْ), following 20:53's paths and rain with the animal's grazing. | terra: People eat and pasture their livestock in the vegetation brought out along the earth's roads; human and mount are provisioned together.
terra: Whoever turns away from the reminder will carry a وِزْر on Resurrection Day; the section's physical load makes this otherwise moral burden perceptible.
terra: The bearer remains under that burden and it is an evil load on Resurrection Day; this verse supplies the enduring pressure of the وِزْر introduced in 20:100.

luna: The source pairs a camel's road with its pace; this ayah places paths among the earth's mountains so people may be guided, echoing both route and the elevated landscape of 88:19. | terra: Broad passes are made through the mountains as roads so people may be guided; it gives the caravan a traversable opening through raised terrain.

luna: The source's final turn is toward the Lord with desire; this ayah says the prophets hastened to good deeds and called on God with hope and fear (رَغَبًا وَرَهَبًا), joining effort and longing. | terra: The prophets call upon God رَغَبًا وَرَهَبًا, in longing and fear; رغبة here is directed devotional orientation rather than the source dictionary's wide stride.

luna: The source's dictionary branches of وَضَعَ include lowering and resting a mount; this ayah says every pregnant woman sets down her burden (تَضَعُ كُلُّ ذَاتِ حَمْلٍ حَمْلَهَا), a bodily reversal of a load carried along a road. | terra: At the Hour every pregnant creature lays down its حمل; putting down a carried load here marks cosmic terror rather than relief granted along the road.

luna: The source's travel-worn camel becomes an explicit pilgrimage mount here: people come on lean camels (ضَامِرٍ) from distant passes, linking bodily wear to a purposeful journey toward worship. | terra: Pilgrims arrive “on every lean camel” from every distant pass; the animal's leanness after a long road directly realizes the source-section sense of a camel worn thin by journeys.

luna: After the source's distant-camel pilgrimage, this ayah says pilgrims mention God's name over grazing livestock and feed the needy; it supplies the devotional and charitable purpose of the arrival.
luna: The source turns the road toward the Lord into an arrival; this adjacent pilgrimage ayah contributes the rites to be completed and the circumambulation of the Ancient House.

luna: The source's camel is a useful mount that prompts remembrance of the Lord; here camels are God's signs, lined up for sacrifice while His name is mentioned, a ritual boundary for the same animal. | terra: The sacrificial camels stand in ordered rows while God's name is pronounced, then fall upon their sides and feed others; posture, animal provision, remembrance, and lowering all meet in one scene.
terra: The animals are subjected to people so they may magnify God for His guidance and give thanks; tractability again leads the rider or handler to remembrance of the Giver.
terra: God subjects what is on earth and makes ships run by His command, closing with divine compassion and mercy; the moving vehicle is fitted and sustained as a gift.
terra: God places no constriction in the religion and names Abraham as forefather; the road toward Him is fitted rather than made impassable.

luna: The source hears a caravan mount in the surah's back; this ayah explicitly says people are carried on animals and ships, placing the loaded animal beside sea travel. | terra: People are carried on livestock and ships; the verse states transport as the shared gift behind the section's mount and the paired vehicles of 43:12.
terra: After settling on the ark, the rider is commanded to praise God for deliverance; arriving and becoming established upon a vehicle elicit the remembrance voiced in 43:13.
terra: The prayer asks “My Lord, cause me to land at a blessed landing”; Rabb is invoked as the one who grants the journey its good stopping-place.
terra: God creates creatures that move on bellies, two legs, and four; the four-footed gait places the section's careful transfer of the animal's limbs within a wider created order.

luna: The source dictionary's ظ ه ر branch uses noon for the camels' daily watering; this ayah names the noon privacy/rest period (مِنَ الظَّهِيرَةِ), giving the camel's water stop a human midday counterpart. | terra: The verse's الظَّهِيرَة fixes the noon-time sense embedded in the source dictionary's ظاهرة, “camels coming to water daily at noon”; the Qur'anic context itself concerns household privacy rather than watering.
terra: The servants of the Merciful walk upon the earth هَوْنًا, gently; this human gait is the moral analogue of the section's calm, easy-going mount.
terra: Noah and his companions are saved in a laden ship; a heavily loaded conveyance becomes the means by which its passengers reach safety.

luna: The source describes camels coming to water; Salih's she-camel has an appointed drinking turn (شِرْبٍ), an explicit counterpart to water being measured for animals. | terra: The she-camel has a fixed drinking turn and the people theirs on a known day; this is the section's daily watering-place rendered as an apportioned schedule.

luna: Where the source's caravan depends on the camel's water stop, Salih commands his people not to harm the she-camel; this makes care for the watering animal a boundary before its slaughter. | terra: They are warned not to harm the she-camel after her drinking share is fixed; the verse marks the boundary around the watering gift.

luna: The source's camel is preserved as a working mount; here the people hamstring the she-camel after the shared watering arrangement, a stark reversal of animal care. | terra: They hamstring her and then regret it; the water-sharing order of 26:155 is destroyed by the people it sustained.

luna: The source's camel is watered on the road; Moses reaches a well where shepherds water their flocks and two women hold theirs back (تَذُودَانِ), a concrete human-and-herd water stop. | terra: Moses reaches Midian's water and finds a community watering their herds while two women hold theirs back; it is a full pastoral water-stop scene.

luna: After watering the flocks, Moses turns to shade and asks his Lord for whatever good He sends; this brings the source's completed task and turning toward the Lord into a single travel-side scene. | terra: Moses waters the women's animals and then withdraws to shade; watering followed by departure closely parallels the section's camels leaving the water.
terra: After Moses waters the animals, one woman returns with an invitation from her father to reward that service; the water-stop leads the traveler toward shelter and recompense.
terra: They will carry their loads and further loads with them; the repeated حمل image turns wrongdoing into an accumulating caravan burden.
luna: The source's route ends by turning toward the Lord; Abraham says he is migrating to his Lord (إِنِّي مُهَاجِرٌ إِلَىٰ رَبِّي), making a real departure and its divine destination explicit.

luna: The source's camel bears provisions and people along the road; this ayah reverses that image with creatures that carry no provision of their own, whom God still sustains along with people. | terra: Many creatures do not carry their own provision, yet God sustains them and humans; this reverses the load-bearing beast and separates carrying from being provided for.
terra: When people board a ship they call upon God sincerely, but after rescue to land they associate partners; the mounted remembrance of 43:13-14 is abandoned at journey's end.
luna: The source's effort is directed toward its Lord; this ayah says those who strive for God are guided to His paths, joining exertion to divine wayfinding.
terra: God sends winds so ships may sail, travelers may seek His bounty, and they may give thanks; easy movement leads to provision and remembrance.

terra: A mother carries her child through weakness upon weakness, gratitude is commanded, and the destination is “to Me”; borne weight, exhaustion, thanks, and divine arrival form the section's sequence in human terms.
terra: The prohibition on swaggering over the earth supplies the proud gait against which 31:19's measured walk, and the section's easy pace, are heard.
terra: “Be measured in your walk and lower your voice” joins moderated pace to controlled sound, matching both the easy gait and the travel sounds developed in the section.
terra: Ships sail through the sea by God's favor, displaying signs to the steadfast and grateful; the moving vehicle is read as a blessing rather than a neutral tool.

luna: The source's caravan needs pasture after water; this ayah describes rain brought to barren land producing crops eaten by people's livestock, repeating that provision cycle. | terra: Water is driven to barren land and produces crops eaten by both livestock and people; divine provision restores the terrain needed by the travelling herd.
terra: The heavens, earth, and mountains refuse the Trust, but the human being carries it; an immense nonphysical charge is made intelligible as a borne load.

luna: The source's caravan follows a road with a place to stop; this ayah places towns between the blessed cities and apportions travel between them (وَقَدَّرْنَا فِيهَا السَّيْرَ), describing measured stages and safe day-and-night movement. | terra: The blessed towns have visible, measured stages between them, and travelers are told to journey by night and day in safety; this is a divinely fitted caravan road with successive stopping-places.

luna: The source's road has a watering place where the caravan remains; this sequel has Saba ask for far-separated journeys (بَاعِدْ بَيْنَ أَسْفَارِنَا), a specific reversal of connected, safely measured stages. | terra: The people ask for their journey-stages to be lengthened, then are scattered; rejection turns the measured, safe route of 34:18 into distance and dispersal.
terra: Ships cleave the two seas so people may seek God's bounty and give thanks; travel, provision, and gratitude again share one vehicle-scene.

luna: Like 6:164, this ayah says no bearer carries another's burden and that return is to the Lord; beside the source's load-bearing camel, it marks moral responsibility as a load that cannot be handed to a mount. | terra: A heavily laden soul may call for help, yet none of its load is carried; this sets the limit of the section's mercy-image of a creature carrying another's weight.

luna: The source dictionary branch B004 of ن ص ب calls bodily weariness nasab; this ayah says no nasab touches the residents of the Garden, making the final resting place a reversal of the road's fatigue. | terra: The “abode of lasting residence” is the reached station where لَا يَمَسُّنَا فِيهَا نَصَبٌ; destination, permanent stay, and the ending of road-fatigue coincide.
terra: Human offspring are carried in the laden ship, الْفُلْكِ الْمَشْحُونِ; this transfers the section's load-bearing vehicle from camel-back to a vessel filled for travel.
terra: God creates for people counterparts to the laden ship that they ride; the neighbouring verses explicitly connect a loaded vehicle with other rideable conveyances.

luna: The source's tame, rideable beast is echoed by cattle made submissive (سَخَّرْنَاهَا لَهُمْ), some of which people ride; it makes the animal's fitness for carrying human beings explicit. | terra: God makes livestock tractable, ذَلَّلْنَاهَا لَهُمْ, so some become their rides; this directly corresponds to the section's compliant, easily guided mount.

luna: This continuation adds milk and other benefits to the subdued animals of 36:72, completing the source's picture of the mount as a providential animal. | terra: The subdued livestock provide further benefits and drinks; riding in 36:72 is thus surrounded by the same provision and watering that sustain the section's road.
luna: The source makes “to your Lord” the caravan's destination; Abraham says he is going to his Lord and expects guidance, joining travel, divine direction, and arrival.
terra: Jonah flees to the laden ship; the same full vehicle that can signify rescue here begins a journey undertaken in flight.
terra: Fine, swift horses are presented to Solomon in the evening; this directly supplies the section's horse, rider, and elevated pace.
terra: Solomon's attention to the good horses is explicitly related to remembrance of his Lord; the mounted animal and zikr meet, though the precise force of his statement is debated.
terra: Solomon has the horses returned and reaches toward their legs and necks; whatever the disputed action, the verse keeps attention on the ridden animal's very limbs and neck.
terra: Job names نُصْبٍ وَعَذَابٍ as the affliction that touched him; the root heard as all-day travel here retains its bodily weariness.
terra: The repeated rule that no bearer bears another's load is followed by “to your Lord is your return,” again joining burden-accounting to arrival at Rabb.

luna: Like the source's ready riding beast, these cattle are made for people to ride and to eat from; this adds the animal's provision to its transport role. | terra: God makes livestock so that people may ride some and eat from others; the riding animal is explicitly a divine provision.

luna: The source makes a camel a means of reaching the road's destination; this ayah says people reach needs they hold in their breasts by riding cattle and are carried on them and ships. | terra: Livestock meet needs carried in human breasts, and people are carried on them and on ships; need, load, and conveyance complete 40:79's gift.

luna: The source makes the surah a road journey; this ayah says God made paths in the earth so people might be guided, immediately before 43:12–14 names the mounts and their destination. | terra: God makes the earth a cradle and puts roads in it so people may be guided; it lays out the traversable ground immediately before 43:12-14's mounts and travel prayer.

luna: This ayah names ships and livestock as things people ride, the exact transport scene that lets the source hear the surah's “back” as a mount rather than only a body part. | terra: God makes ships and livestock into things people ride; this supplies the actual mounts whose backs, remembrance, and homeward orientation are developed in 43:13-14.

luna: The source's camel-back reading meets the ayah's “on their backs” (ظُهُورِهَا): riders are to remember their Lord for this provision, so mounting and remembrance form one scene. | terra: Settling on the mounts' ظُهُورِهِ and remembering the Lord's blessing joins the section's mount-back, rider, divine gift, and zikr in one act.

luna: The rider's utterance in the source continues in this ayah: “we are returning to our Lord” (لَمُنقَلِبُونَ), making the journey's destination part of the mount's remembrance. | terra: The mounted travel prayer ends “to our Lord we are returning,” exactly joining a ride to the section's road whose destination is Rabb.

luna: The source's وَضَعَ dictionary branches describe lowering or setting a mount down; this ayah says a mother carries her child in hardship and lays him down in hardship, shifting the heavy-load image from a beast's back to gestation and birth. | terra: The mother حَمَلَتْهُ كُرْهًا وَوَضَعَتْهُ كُرْهًا, carrying and laying down in hardship; the section's load and its removal are joined in one bodily ordeal.
terra: حَتَّىٰ تَضَعَ الْحَرْبُ أَوْزَارَهَا makes war lay down its burdens; the section's paired “put down” and “load” reappears as the ending of conflict.

luna: The source's camel completes a road to a place of rest; this ayah says the sacrificial offering was held back from reaching its place (مَعْكُوفًا أَنْ يَبْلُغَ مَحِلَّهُ), showing the animal's route interrupted before arrival.
terra: The oath by “those bearing a load,” فَالْحَامِلَاتِ وِقْرًا, isolates the section's first caravan feature: a bearer defined by what rests upon it.
terra: The next oath, فَالْجَارِيَاتِ يُسْرًا, makes easy motion follow load-bearing, the same sequence as the laden animal whose gait becomes tractable.
terra: The scrolls' rule that no laden soul bears another's burden supplies another direct boundary for who can carry the section's load.
terra: “To your Lord is the final limit” gives the section's caravan-road its ultimate terminus in the same direct second-person address.
terra: God says the Quran has been made easy for remembrance; the source-section quality of an easily guided, quickly responsive mount becomes an analogy for accessible instruction.
terra: The repeated declaration that the Quran is made easy reinforces ease as an enacted divine making, not merely a favorable circumstance.

luna: The source gives the camel a central place in the road image; this passage calls Salih's she-camel a trial and commands watchfulness, turning the animal itself into a sign. | terra: The she-camel is sent as a trial, and the prophet must watch and be patient; the mount-like animal is here a test whose treatment measures the people.

luna: The source's watering stop is measured; this ayah explicitly divides water between the people and the camel by turns, making the camel's drink a public allotment. | terra: The water is divided between the people and the she-camel, each turn attended; it directly stages regulated arrival at water.

luna: The source's caravan needs its camel alive for the road; this continuation says the people called their companion, who hamstrung the camel, reversing the shared watering order of 54:28. | terra: They call their companion and hamstring the she-camel; this is the violent undoing of the apportioned watering scene in 54:28.
terra: The third refrain again presents remembered revelation as something God renders tractable, echoing the section's compliant conveyance.
terra: The final repetition keeps ease tied to remembrance, linking the section's easy movement back to the rider's zikr in 43:13.
terra: God رَفَعَ the sky and وَضَعَ the balance; the section's low and raised paces appear here as a deliberately paired cosmic ordering.
terra: The Event is خَافِضَةٌ رَّافِعَةٌ, lowering and raising; this compact reversal illuminates the two opposed levels heard in the animal's gait.
luna: The source's camel drinks on its route; this passage contrasts that sustaining stop with scalding water for the condemned, setting up the thirsty-camel comparison of 56:55.

luna: The source presents water as a camel's needed provision; this ayah says the condemned drink like thirst-crazed camels, turning that same need into punishment. | terra: The condemned drink boiling water like desperately thirsty camels; the familiar watering-stop becomes insatiable and punitive rather than merciful provision.

luna: The source's ر ف ع branch describes a camel's raised pace; this ayah uses the same root for God raising believers in rank, a different kind of elevation that qualifies the physical gait reading.
terra: The believers did not spur either horses or رِكَاب against these settlements; the very riding-stock named by the source definition appears in a journey explicitly not made.

luna: The source's camel bears useful travel cargo; this ayah compares those who do not carry the Torah's responsibility to a donkey carrying books, making weight without understanding the opposite of purposeful transport. | terra: The donkey carrying books bears a real load without receiving their guidance; it exposes the boundary between transporting weight and inwardly carrying meaning.
luna: The source says that when one task is finished, another should begin; this ayah commands leaving trade and hastening to God's remembrance, while 62:10 gives the return to ordinary work.

luna: After the source's “when you are free, then toil,” this ayah sends people back into the land to seek God's bounty and remember Him, completing the work-and-remembrance sequence begun in 62:9. | terra: Once the prayer is finished, believers disperse through the land, seek God's bounty, and remember Him often; completed devotion opens into productive movement without losing zikr.
terra: Whoever is mindful of God is granted يُسْرًا in his affair; ease is made as a consequence of right orientation.

luna: The source pairs a hard mount with an easy one; this ayah promises ease after hardship (عُسْرٍ يُسْرًا), adding a temporal passage from difficulty to ease. | terra: سَيَجْعَلُ اللَّهُ بَعْدَ عُسْرٍ يُسْرًا states the hard-to-easy passage as a divinely made succession, matching the section's resistant and tractable mounts.
luna: The source's journey moves toward the Lord; this ayah tells people to walk the earth's slopes (مَنَاكِبِهَا), seek provision, and remember that resurrection is to Him.

luna: The source dictionary branch for ن ص ب describes upright exertion; this verse instead uses نُصُبٍ for a set-up marker that crowds rush toward, a distinct lexical branch and a different endpoint from the source's road toward the Lord. | terra: People emerge rapidly as though rushing toward a نُصُب; the section's root for sustained travel becomes an erected goal approached at an ominous pace.

luna: The source's wide-striding horse and broad road need open ground; this ayah says God spread the earth out, while 71:20 completes the purpose as travel along wide paths. | terra: The earth is made an expanse for people, preparing the broad movement named in the next verse.

luna: The source names a broad road for a caravan; this ayah explicitly says people may travel through wide paths (سُبُلًا فِجَاجًا), making the route's breadth concrete. | terra: People travel through its فِجَاجًا سُبُلًا, broad passes as roads; this corresponds to the section's wide-stepping animal and ample way.
terra: The prophetic addressee has “a long movement/occupation” by day; it corresponds to the section's all-day exertion before renewed devotion.
terra: After the long daytime occupation of 73:7, the Prophet is told to remember his Lord's name and devote himself wholly to Him; exertion resolves into directed Godward attention.

luna: The source describes a whole day's walk and effort; this ayah recognizes people traveling through the land seeking God's bounty and makes the devotional burden responsive to what is easy for them.
terra: The trumpet ushers in يَوْمٌ عَسِيرٌ; hardship here is the destination-day itself rather than a difficult mount that can become easy.
terra: That hard day is عَلَى الْكَافِرِينَ غَيْرُ يَسِيرٍ; explicit denial of ease fixes the far boundary of the section's promised tractability.
luna: The source contrasts a difficult untrained mount with a tame, readily guided one; this simile shows wild asses (حُمُرٌ مُّسْتَنفِرَةٌ) fleeing from a reminder, an opposite animal response.
luna: This continuation supplies the lion that startles the wild asses in 74:50; the source's trainable riding beast follows a guide, while these animals flee a pursuer.
terra: إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ يَوْمَئِذٍ الْمُسْتَقَرُّ names the Lord as the final settled place, closely matching the caravan's destination where it remains.
terra: Hell's thrown sparks are likened to tawny camels; the familiar road animal becomes the scale and shape of a terrifying projectile rather than a merciful conveyance.

luna: The source's camels rest at pasture and come to water; this ayah pairs the earth's water and pasture (مَاءَهَا وَمَرْعَىٰهَا), showing the two necessities of that stop. | terra: God brings the earth's water and pasture out of it; these are the two provisions at which the section's travelling animal drinks and remains.
terra: The mountains are firmly set between the water-and-pasture verse and the declaration of provision; they form the fixed terrain through which the caravan moves.

luna: The source names pasture as a place for camels to remain; this ayah identifies the pasture and cattle as provision for people and their herds, completing 79:31's water-and-grass scene. | terra: Water, pasture, and fixed mountains are declared provision for people and their livestock; traveler and mount receive the road's resources together.
luna: The command to consider food opens the sequence that ends with pasture for livestock in 80:31–32, supplying the source's grazing camel with an account of its provision.

luna: The source's camel must stop for water before continuing; this food sequence begins with rain poured down (صَبًّا), whose neighboring verses 80:26 and 31–32 show the earth producing pasture for livestock.
luna: This ayah says the earth is split open in the provision sequence that leads to the source's pasture scene; 80:31–32 identify its yield as fodder and provision for cattle.
luna: Grain is the first named crop in this sequence; the source's camel rests at pasture, and 80:31–32 complete how the earth's growth feeds livestock.
luna: Grapes and green growth are another stage in the sequence leading to pasture; 80:31–32 name fodder and its provision for livestock, connecting growth to the source's feeding stop.
luna: Olives and date palms extend the food sequence whose endpoint is pasture for animals in 80:31–32, matching the source's image of a journey sustained by animal fodder.
luna: Dense gardens continue the earth's provision sequence; 80:31–32 complete it with fodder and provision for livestock, the pasture behind the source's camel stop.

luna: The source's dictionary entry names a camel resting in pasture; this ayah names fruit and fodder (أَبًّا) among what the earth brings forth, and 80:32 says it is provision for people and livestock. | terra: Fruit and herbage are brought forth in the food passage; the herbage supplies the grazing side of the section's stopping-place.

luna: The source explicitly places camels at pasture; this ayah names pasture's yield as enjoyment and provision for people and livestock (لَكُمْ وَلِأَنْعَامِكُمْ). | terra: The vegetation is provision for people and their livestock; road companions share what the land produces.

luna: The source's camel is tended, loaded, and ridden; this ayah pictures valuable pregnant camels left unattended at the Last Hour, reversing human care for a working beast. | terra: The prized pregnant she-camels are abandoned at the Hour; the ordered, useful caravan dissolves so completely that even its most valued animals are left.

luna: The source says to toil and then turn toward the Lord; this ayah describes a person laboring toward their Lord (كَادِحٌ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ) until meeting Him, making road-work and return explicit. | terra: The human being labors “toward your Lord” and will meet Him; exertion, direction, and arrival reproduce the section's whole road in one address.
luna: The source's mount rests at pasture; this ayah says God brings forth pasture (الْمَرْعَىٰ) and then makes it dark, dried stubble, adding the grass's passing cycle to the route.
luna: This continuation makes the pasture of 87:4 wither into dark stubble; it sets the source's grazing stop within a cycle of provision that does not last.

luna: The source's yielding mount represents ease; this divine promise says “We will ease you toward ease” (لِلْيُسْرَىٰ), carrying the same root into a promise about the addressed servant's course. | terra: God tells the same prophetic addressee وَنُيَسِّرُكَ لِلْيُسْرَى; divine preparation makes the traveler fit for the easy course rather than merely promising ease around him.

luna: The source explicitly asks the reader to look at the camel; this ayah asks how camels (الْإِبِلِ) were created, making the same animal a sign for reflection. | terra: The command to look at the camel makes the section's load-bearing mount itself an object of reflective attention.

luna: The source's root ر ف ع names the camel's quicker raised gait; this next question asks how the sky was raised (رُفِعَتْ), extending the look from camel movement to the heavens. | terra: Immediately above the camel scene, the sky is رُفِعَتْ; the section hears this same root as the mount's raised pace.

luna: The source's root ن ص ب names exertion and an upright stance; this continuation asks how mountains were erected (نُصِبَتْ), shifting the same posture word to the landscape. | terra: The mountains are نُصِبَتْ in the next view; this turns the section's root for sustained travel and fatigue into the firmly erected landmarks of its landscape.

luna: This continuation asks how the earth was spread out, completing the camel-sky-mountain-earth sequence and giving the source's caravan road an opened landscape. | terra: The earth is spread out beneath the camel, raised sky, and erected mountains; it completes the road-landscape of 88:17-19.
terra: The reassured soul is told to return to its Lord, pleased and pleasing; arrival at Rabb is an invited homecoming.
terra: Humanity is created in toil, كَبَد; it gives the section's road-weariness a general human analogue without specifying travel.
luna: The source contrasts two camel paces, easy and difficult; this ayah says people have been shown two paths (النَّجْدَيْنِ), opening a moral choice later pictured as an uphill pass.

luna: Where the source has sustained travel and exertion, this ayah says the person did not attempt the difficult pass (الْعَقَبَةَ); 90:12–17 explain the hard ascent as costly acts of care and faith.
luna: This ayah asks what the steep pass is, naming a difficult route; 90:13–17 supply its concrete acts, giving the source's hard road a moral counterpart.
luna: The source's difficult road requires exertion; this ayah names freeing a slave as one act on the steep pass, while 90:14–17 complete the costly path.
luna: This ayah adds feeding on a day of hunger to the steep pass; it connects the source's loaded journey to provision for the hungry, with 90:15–17 completing the passage.
luna: This ayah specifies feeding an orphan who is a near relative as one part of the steep pass, making the source's road-work an act of care; 90:16–17 continue the path.
luna: This ayah names feeding a destitute person in misery on the steep pass; the source's strenuous route is thus paralleled by costly care, completed by the faith and patience of 90:17.
luna: This ayah completes the steep-pass sequence with faith, patience, and mercy, giving the source's effort toward the Lord a moral destination after the concrete acts in 90:13–16.
luna: This ayah identifies those who took the steep pass as people of the right; it supplies the outcome of the difficult path described in 90:11–17, beside the source's road toward its Lord.

luna: The source links a camel with the Lord and the road; Salih identifies God's she-camel and her turn to drink, joining divine claim to the animal and its water. | terra: The messenger says “Allah's she-camel and her drink”; animal, divine ownership, and the protected water-share are compressed into one warning.

luna: The source's camel remains a working companion on the road; this next ayah says the people denied the warning and hamstrung her, the opposite outcome. | terra: They deny the messenger and hamstring Allah's she-camel; rejection destroys both the animal and the protected drink named in 91:13.
luna: The source's easy and difficult mounts embody opposite routes; this passage begins by naming giving and God-consciousness, with 92:7 completing its consequence as ease made accessible.
luna: This continuation affirms the best reward after giving; 92:7 says such a person is eased toward ease, echoing the source's contrast between a tame, yielding mount and a difficult one.

luna: The source root ي س ر describes an easy-to-follow mount; here God eases (فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ) the giver toward ease, making the mount's obedient movement a moral path. | terra: فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْيُسْرَى portrays the rightly oriented person as being made ready for ease, like the section's responsive animal made fit to proceed.
luna: The opposite sequence begins with withholding and self-sufficiency; 92:10 completes it by easing that person toward hardship, reversing the source's yielding, easy mount.
luna: This ayah adds denial of the best reward to the withholding sequence; 92:10 completes the consequence as a path made easy toward hardship, the source's difficult route in a moral register.

luna: The source contrasts an untrained, difficult mount with one easy to guide; here the one who withholds is eased toward hardship (لِلْعُسْرَىٰ), making difficulty a path shaped by conduct. | terra: فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْعُسْرَى deliberately couples facilitation with the hard end; it exposes that the road one is made ready for can itself be difficulty.
terra: “To your Lord is the return” restates the section's final direction, though without an accompanying travel scene.

luna: The source dictionary branch of ص د ر describes camels departing from water; this ayah uses يَصْدُرُ for people dispersing to see their deeds, a different setting but a specific echo of leaving a stopping place for what follows. | terra: يَصْدُرُ النَّاسُ أَشْتَاتًا pictures people issuing forth in separate groups; the source dictionary sense “camels depart the water” supplies a concrete herd-motion behind the verb.

luna: The source's image includes a camel's slow, burdened road and a horse's broad gait; this oath instead opens with chargers panting at speed, an alternate mounted pace whose identification as horses is traditional rather than stated here. | terra: The panting chargers stage the elevated, exhausting pace opposite the section's easy and gentle animal gait.

luna: The source's riding animal carries people and loads; this next image has the chargers strike sparks with their hooves, continuing the high-speed mounted scene of 100:1. | terra: The chargers strike sparks, giving the fast gait a hoof-beat intensity absent from the calm caravan pace.

luna: The source's caravan travels to reach a destination; these chargers rush at dawn in a raid, giving the contrasting mounted speed a military purpose. | terra: Their dawn charge turns animal movement from measured travel into attack.

luna: The source's road is a sustained caravan path; this continuation raises dust in the chargers' passage, extending the raid scene begun in 100:1–3. | terra: The charge raises a cloud of dust; the road itself registers the violence of the faster tempo.

luna: The source's camel reaches a settled destination; this final line says the chargers penetrate into the midst of a host, completing the contrast with a forceful arrival. | terra: The riders penetrate the center of a host; this supplies the destination of the rapid mounted sequence, a hostile gathering rather than rest with Rabb.

luna: This ayah names Quraysh's settled security (إِيلَافِ قُرَيْشٍ); 106:2 specifies the seasonal journeys whose reliable rhythm gives the source's recurring caravan travel a close historical parallel. | terra: Quraysh's cultivated familiarity anchors the two seasonal caravan journeys of 106:2 as an established communal rhythm.

luna: The source turns the surah into a caravan journey; this ayah names Quraysh's regular winter and summer journeys, an explicit parallel of recurring travel by caravan. | terra: The winter and summer caravan journeys make recurrent travel itself the community's ordered livelihood.

luna: The source's mount leads to remembrance of the Lord; after 106:2 names Quraysh's journeys, this ayah directs them to worship the Lord of the House, setting devotion as the caravan's response. | terra: After naming the two journeys, the passage commands worship of the Lord of the House; the caravan road is given its Rabb and destination.

luna: The source presents animal travel as mercy and provision; this closing ayah says the Lord feeds Quraysh against hunger and secures them from fear, completing the journey-and-worship sequence of 106:2–3. | terra: That Lord feeds against hunger and secures against fear; the journey's provision and safety explain why its destination is remembered as gift.
